section.title: P versus NP asks whether recognizing a solution makes finding it easy
section.deck: Avi Wigderson uses a computational question to explore the difference between discovery and verification.

blocks.question: What is P versus NP, and why connect it to the limits of human knowledge?
answer: Wigderson deliberately gives an intuitive explanation rather than a formal definition. Computer science studies which problems computers can solve, and efficient algorithms turn some questions into things we can actually know. A navigation application is his example: an efficient shortest-path algorithm makes a useful answer available rather than merely imaginable.

He describes P through efficient solution-finding and NP through efficient checking: even when we do not know how to find an answer, someone might supply a proposed solution whose validity is comparatively easy to verify. The distinction is between discovering the answer and recognizing that an answer is good. NP in this explanation does not mean a class known to be impossible or necessarily hard to solve.

To connect this to human inquiry, he argues that a serious search normally has some way to recognize success. A mathematician can inspect a proposed proof; a scientist can compare a theory with observations; an engineer can check whether a design satisfies the assigned constraints. His examples include physical and monetary constraints, so a design that violates them fails even if it is impressive in other respects.

Wigderson interprets these activities through the discovery-versus-verification lens and asks what would change if efficiently recognizable solutions were also efficiently findable. In that philosophical framing, P equaling NP would collapse a major barrier between what we want to know and what we can discover. His expansive examples, including scientific cures, convey the scale of the question; they are not a claim that the clip supplies a practical algorithm for every human problem. The interview does not resolve P versus NP or establish a literal formal classification of all human endeavors.
